title: "Analyzing the Media of a Favorite Game"
description: "Seminar worksheet · Take the media of a game apart in three steps: list them by channel, name the job of each one, and decide which sounds are inside or outside the game world."
seminar: 1

format: lesson-typst

::: {.lead}
A player meets all the media of a game at the same time: a theme tune, a
flash of light, a line of dialogue, a health bar that turns red. A media
designer must take this experience apart. Today there are no new ideas:
you use what Lecture 1 taught in three steps on a game you play yourself:
list the media by channel, name the job of each one, and decide whether a
sound is inside or outside the game world. Do each activity alone. The
results of the activities are at the end of this worksheet.
:::

## Recall

- Digital media: text, images, audio, video, animation and interactive
  content.
- The **tetrad**: mechanics, story, aesthetics and technology make the
  player experience together.
- Media do five jobs: **feedback**, **guidance**, **mood**, **story**,
  **identity**.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 1 · Recall"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="technology|post-production"}
A chime and a flash when the player collects a coin. Which job?
:   feedback

    Why: It tells the player what the action did.

Which element of the tetrad are the events of the game?
:   story

    Why: The story is the events, written in advance or made by play.

A glowing door at the end of a dark room. Which job?
:   guidance

    Why: It shows the player where to go.
:::
:::

## Activity 1 · A media inventory

The first step of an analysis is to describe, not to judge: an
**inventory** lists all the media of a game by **channel**.

- **Visual:** the art style, characters, places, animation, effects.
- **Audio:** music, sound effects, voices, **ambience** (the background
  sound of a place, such as wind or rain).
- **Text and story:** dialogue, item names, the story in words.
- **Cinematic:** cut-scenes, intro videos, trailers.
- **Interface:** menus, buttons, icons, the HUD (health, score, time).

![The screen of Ember Trail: each number marks one media element.](images/annotated-screen.png){width=90%}

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 1 · Your inventory · 12 min"}
Choose a game on your phone and take a screenshot of one busy moment.

1. Make a table: element, channel, when it appears.
2. Write at least six rows; use all five channels if you can.

*Your product:* the screenshot and the table. Keep both for Activity 2.

::: {.check}
A good table looks like: "the hero in a cartoon style (visual, always); the
battle music (audio, in fights); the health bar (interface, always); the
line 'The gate is locked!' (text and story, at the gate); the intro film
(cinematic, at the start); the sound of rain (audio, in the forest)."

- ☐ Six rows or more.
- ☐ Each row has a channel and a moment.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 2 · Which channel?"}
Choose the media channel.

::: {.match extra="technology"}
The soft, round shapes of all the characters.
:   visual

    Why: The art style is part of the visual channel.

The sound of wind in the forest.
:   audio

    Why: Ambience is part of the audio channel.

A short film between two chapters.
:   cinematic

    Why: The player watches instead of playing.

The health bar and the coin counter.
:   interface

    Why: The HUD is part of the interface.
:::
:::

## Activity 2 · The job of each element

An analysis goes further than a list. For each element it says its **job**
and its **effect on the player**:

- "There is music in the menu" only describes.
- "The slow flute music in the menu makes the player calm before play
  begins" names the element, its job (mood) and its effect.
- One element often has several jobs: a trumpet tune at the end of a level
  is feedback, mood and identity.

![One coin, three jobs.](images/media-functions.png){width=90%}

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 2 · Three sentences · 10 min"}
Use the inventory of your game. Choose three elements, and write for each
one its job (or jobs) and one sentence about its effect on the player.

*Your product:* three analytic sentences.

::: {.check}
A good sentence looks like: "The red flash of the screen when the hero is
hit is feedback: it tells me at once that I lost health, so I play more
carefully."

- ☐ Each sentence names the element, its job and its effect.
- ☐ The three elements come from different channels.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 3 · Which job?"}
Choose the main job.

::: {.match extra="technology"}
Slow strings and rain sounds in a sad scene.
:   mood

    Why: They set how the moment should feel.

An old statue that shows how the village was destroyed.
:   story

    Why: It tells what happened, without words.

A short theme tune that players know from the first second.
:   identity

    Why: It tells which game this is.
:::
:::

## Activity 3 · Inside or outside the game world?

An element is **diegetic** when it belongs to the game world, so that the
characters could see or hear it: a campfire's crackle, footsteps, a radio
in a room. It is **non-diegetic** when only the player notices it: the
background music, the score, the health bar. The test is one question:
*could a character in the world notice it?*

![Inside or outside the game world.](images/diegesis.png){width=80%}

{{< sim file="sims/sound-stage.html" poster="sims/sound-stage.png" title="Sound Stage: inside or outside the world?" kind="game" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
Do not judge by whether a sound changes. The wind does not change when the
fox walks, but the fox could hear it: it is diegetic.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 3 · Sound Stage · 10 min"}
Open **Sound Stage** (headphones if you can). Walk the fox past the
campfire, and switch each layer on and off.

1. List the elements that the fox could notice (diegetic).
2. List the elements that only the player notices (non-diegetic).

*Your product:* two lists.

::: {.check}
Diegetic: the footsteps, the campfire's crackle, the wind. Non-diegetic:
the flute music, the health bar and the name tag above the fox. The
crackle gets louder near the fire because it comes from a place in the
world; the wind stays the same, but it is diegetic too.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 4 · Diegetic or not?"}
Choose the right answer. You can use an answer more than once.

::: {.match extra="feedback"}
The fox's footsteps.
:   diegetic

    Why: The fox could hear its own steps.

The flute music of Ember Trail.
:   non-diegetic

    Why: There is no flute in the forest.

The wind in the trees, which does not change.
:   diegetic

    Why: The fox could hear it, even though it never changes.

The coin counter in the corner.
:   non-diegetic

    Why: Only the player sees it.
:::
:::

## Case study: analysing Ember Trail

*Ember Trail* is a made-up 2D adventure game for phones. A young fox crosses
a forest at night to go home. The art style is soft and round, the colours
are warm against deep blue, and the music is a solo flute with wind sounds.
The interface shows health, coins and a pause button. Short animated scenes
tell the story between chapters. The Game challenge of the interactive page
analyses it with the method of this seminar. In the mini-game below, the
fox walks through the forest, and you tap the media elements that each
order asks for.

{{< sim file="sims/ember-trail.html" poster="sims/ember-trail.png" title="Ember Trail: media hunt" kind="game" height="600" >}}

## Exercises

1. Name the five media channels of a game.
2. What is ambience? Give an example.
3. Turn this description into an analysis: "There is rain in level 3."
4. Can one element have several jobs? Give an example.
5. What is the difference between diegetic and non-diegetic?
6. The wind in a forest never changes. Is it diegetic? Why?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Visual, audio, text and story, cinematic, interface.
2. The background sound of a place, for example rain or wind.
3. For example: "The rain sound in level 3 sets a sad mood, so the player
   feels alone."
4. Yes: a trumpet tune at the end of a level is feedback, mood and
   identity.
5. Diegetic: the characters could notice it; non-diegetic: only the player
   notices it.
6. Yes: the characters could hear it, even if it never changes.
:::
